ta-l1d39q2-d1e97.summary: The Prooemium of the second question of Distinction 39 turns to divine providence and announces two articles: what it is, and whether it is of all things.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e109.summary: First argument that providence belongs to knowledge. Boethius says providence is so called because God sees far off as from the watchtower of eternity, and seeing belongs to knowledge.
claims: Providence is seeing.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e112.summary: Second argument that it belongs to omnipotence. Wis. 14:3 says 'you, Father, govern all by providence', and governing belongs to power (Heb. 1:3, 'upholding all by the word of his power').
claims: Providence governs.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e121.summary: Third argument that it belongs to will. Damascene says providence is the divine will by which all things receive fitting direction to their end.
claims: Providence is will.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e125.summary: Fourth argument that it is the same as disposition. Boethius says providence is the reason established in the highest prince of all by which he disposes all things.
claims: Providence disposes.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e128.summary: Fifth argument that it is the same as fate. Relation to different things does not diversify essence, and providence and fate differ only so: the mode of governance referred to divine knowledge is providence, referred to the things governed is fate (Boethius).
claims: Providence and fate differ only by relation.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e131.summary: Thomas's determination. Knowledge, disposition, and providence relate by addition. Since God has quasi-practical knowledge of creatures, it is considered like an artisan's. An artisan pre-conceiving his work first considers the end, then the order of the thing to that end and of the parts to one another (foundation under wall, wall under roof), ordered further to the house's end, and third what promotes attaining the end and removes impediments (supports, windows, and the like, fitting it for habitation). This thinking out is called knowledge by cognition alone, of the end and the means; disposition by the order thought out in the work, since disposition means order; providence by what promotes the end, since the provident is one who conjectures well about what helps and hinders the end. So in God, knowledge concerns himself and what he makes; disposition the twofold order he places in things, of thing to thing as they help one another to the last end and of the whole universe to God (as the Philosopher's army ordered among its parts and to the leader's good); providence what he assigns to things so ordered to preserve order and drive out disorder.
claims: Knowledge, disposition, and providence add to one another: cognition, order to the end, and provision of means and removal of obstacles.
Disposition is the order of things to one another and of the universe to God.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e134.summary: Reply to the first argument. Providence and disposition, considered variously, belong to knowledge, will, and power. An artisan may know his works only speculatively without intending to make them, and then his providence and disposition belong only to knowledge; as he orders them to work with the purpose of executing, to knowledge and will; as he executes, to knowledge, will, and power. So in God, the first two are eternal, the third temporal, and the execution of providence is called governance.
claims: Providence belongs to knowledge, will, and power under different aspects; its execution is governance.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e137.summary: This answers the second, third, and fourth arguments, since providence includes disposition and adds to it, which is why one is said to dispose by providence.
claims: Providence includes disposition.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e140.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Providence and fate differ in essence: as a house's form in the artisan's mind is called art and in stones and wood artefact, so the plan of governance has one being in the divine mind, providence, and another in the secondary causes by whose office divine governance is carried out, fate, from 'for, faris' (to speak), either as a kind of utterance of divine ordination, as the spoken word utters the inner concept, or because the ancients used to foretell the future from these causes, chiefly the heavens' motion.
claims: Providence is the plan in God's mind; fate is that plan as realized in secondary causes.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e152.summary: First argument that providence is not of all things. It belongs to providence to remove what impedes the end, and evil is disorder from the end, and there are many evils.
claims: Evil escapes providence.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e155.summary: Second argument. Nothing by chance is provided for, since chance is an unforeseen event, among things done for an end when something else happens than intended, and many things happen by chance (the Philosopher), or else all would be necessary.
claims: Chance events are unprovided.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e158.summary: Third argument. Whatever is provided is ordered to one thing, and free choice is open to either.
claims: Free choice is not determined.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e162.summary: Fourth argument. Whatever is provided attains its end for the most part, unless providence errs, and evil is found for the most part.
claims: Evil prevails.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e165.summary: Fifth argument. Providence orders, and much happens disorderly in nature (rainy summers, dry winters) and among humans (the just punished by the wicked, who prosper).
claims: Disorder in nature and history.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e168.summary: Sixth argument. Hab. 1:14, 'will you make men like the fish of the sea?', marvels at disorder among humans, implying God's providence does not extend to brutes.
claims: Providence does not extend to brutes.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e174.summary: Sed contra from Wis. 12: he has care of all, and care or solicitude signifies providence.
claims: God cares for all.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e177.summary: Thomas's determination. Nearly all wise men have discussed this, so their positions must be seen. Democritus and almost all the ancients, admitting only material causes, held there is no providence and all happens by chance, refuted in philosophy. Others held providence of some things, not all, in two ways. One, attributed to Aristotle though not expressly in his words and expressly held by the Commentator (Metaphysics 11), says providence extends only to species and necessary individuals, since what departs from its course is not under providence, so generable and corruptible particulars are not provided for, God caring for singulars only as sharing a common nature (as a spider knowing how to weave); this removes God's judgement of human works. Another, Rabbi Moses's, adds providence over human individuals and their particular acts, since the individual human has an intellect grasping the species as such and shares with perpetual substances, which are provided for individually, in his nobler part. But since divine knowledge is equally of singulars and universals, and the supremely good orders all to their end as they are apt, it seems unfitting that not all singulars be provided for, and this is against Matt. 10 (not one sparrow falls without the Father). Others hold God provides for all, but some say equally, and fall into three errors: thinking good and evil equally provided, which cannot be intended by one agent, they posit two gods, as the Manichaeans, refuted since evil has no efficient cause and cannot be intended; thinking contingents and necessaries equally provided, they deny free choice and contingency, plainly false; thinking rational and irrational equally provided, they hold nothing bad befalls brutes except as punishment or occasion of reward, so killing a brute is a sin like killing a man, as some heretics of our time seem to think. So all things are subject to providence, but not in the same way. Providence presupposes disposition, which sets order among things preserved in grades of natures, and providence does not destroy that order, so its effect is fulfilled in each thing according to how it is apt to attain its end (Dionysius: providence saves natures, not destroys them). Some things attain their end by nature, others by will besides. Among natural things, some natures cannot be impeded, the higher grade, as heavenly bodies, where nothing happens unintended by God through their defect (Avicenna: no evil above the moon's orb); others can be impeded and fail, the generable and corruptible, which, though lower, are good, and both together are better than one, and if God had given this nature unfailingness it would be another nature, to the detriment of the universe's perfection. So he made it foreknowing its contingent defect, natural evil, but not intending it, and provided that if evil occurs from a nature's defect it is ordered to good, as one's corruption is another's generation; this extends to brutes, acting by natural instinct, whose evils are compensated by a natural good, not by reward, as a fly's death is the spider's food. In nobler creatures there is another principle, will, which the nearer to God the freer from natural necessity (Boethius), so by its condition it can keep the right order toward the end or fail; if it tended to the end inevitably, providence would remove the condition of its nature (Dionysius). So it was made able to fail, with failing or not in its power, unlike natural defect. These defects of wills, beyond the intention of providence, God foreknew and ordered to good, not only of nature but of grace: to the good of justice (fault ordered by punishment), to the good of others' wills, corrected or growing in merit and glory through their wickedness, and much else human reason cannot explain. So good and evil are subject to providence, evil as foreknown and ordered, not intended; good as intended, necessary good so that it cannot fail, contingent so that it can, voluntary so that it has reward or punishment or is ordered to another's, natural so that it attains its natural end if good and yields to another nature's good if evil.
claims: All things are subject to providence, but each according to its nature: necessary, contingent, natural, and voluntary differently.
Evil is foreknown and ordered to good but not intended; natural defects serve other natures, voluntary defects serve justice and others' good.
Against Democritus, Averroes, Maimonides, and the Manichaeans, providence extends to all singulars.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e180.summary: Reply to the first argument. Providence directs each thing to its end and removes impediments while preserving the nature directed to the end, from whose defectible condition evils happen, not from divine intention, which orders those evils to good.
claims: Evils come from defectible natures, which providence preserves.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e184.summary: Reply to the second argument. The effect follows the condition of its proximate cause, so though something is provided by God it is said to happen by chance if beyond the intention of the operating nature, or by fortune if beyond the intention of an agent acting by purpose.
claims: Chance is relative to the proximate cause's intention.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e187.summary: Reply to the third argument. Free choice is of itself ordered to one thing, the good, yet so that it can fail and that this is in its power; if it tended inevitably to one thing, the character of will in such a nature would be removed.
claims: Free choice is ordered to the good but can fail.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e190.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. In natural things evil is in the minority, both in supposits, since natural evil occurs only in the small sphere of generables compared to incorruptible heavenly bodies, and in the same thing, since natural causes attain their effects for the most part. In voluntary things evil is in the minority among angels, since many more remained than fell, perhaps more than all the damned, demons and humans together. In human nature good seems in the minority, for two reasons: the corruption of human nature by original sin, which God foresaw and preordained but did not prevent, lest nature lose its freedom; and the condition of human nature itself. As among natural things there is pure act, without defect, pure potency, prime matter, always deficient unless actualized, and act mixed with privation, working rightly for the most part, so among intellectual natures there is complete act without potency, from which nothing wrong proceeds (God), nature mixed with potency but with a directing act in its nature (angels), failing only rarely, and human nature, whose second perfections directing its works are not innate but acquired or infused, so the human possible intellect is compared to prime matter (Commentator) and a blank tablet (the Philosopher), equally indifferent to all things to understand or do; since evil happens in many ways and good in one (Dionysius), it is bent to evil for the most part. Human nature so considered is a perfect agent only in natural operations; it becomes a perfect agent in all its operations when perfected by second perfections, the virtues, and then it is determined to one thing, for the most part in this life, always in heaven. So Cicero compares virtue to nature, a voluntary habit in the manner of nature consonant with reason, and a will perfected by justice relates to just works as fire to upward motion. So the order of providence is better kept in the good than in the wicked.
claims: Natural and angelic evil is rare; human evil is common because of original sin and because human nature lacks innate directing perfections.
Virtues, acquired or infused, determine human nature to the good like a second nature.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e193.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Everything in the world is ordered, though the reason of the order does not appear to us in some cases, especially voluntary ones, where good and evil befall both the wicked and the good; God knows the reason, as a doctor knows why he gives some sick and healthy people hot remedies and others cold, which amazes the ignorant (Boethius). This disorder, carefully considered, is not found in what human works are per se ordered to, what is per se good or evil: a good work always has its reward in the perfection of virtue, the human good, and in attaining beatitude, and conversely for evil. The mixture occurs in goods outside the human being or not his as human, bodily goods and goods of fortune, yet it is always ordered to the human's per se good, grace or glory (Rom. 8:28, all things work together for good for those who love God), or to the manifestation of divine justice, since the wicked often prosper in this life that their judgement may appear more manifest.
claims: Apparent disorder affects only external goods; virtue and beatitude always reward good works.
God knows the reason of all order, like a physician.

ta-l1d39q2-d1e199.summary: Reply to the sixth argument. That authority suggests providence is not alike for brutes and humans, which is true.
claims: Providence differs for brutes and humans.

ta-l1d39q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium announces two articles on providence: what it is and whether it extends to all things.

ta-l1d39q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 holds that knowledge, disposition, and providence add to one another as in an artisan: cognition of end and means, the order of things to one another and of the universe to God, and the provision of what preserves order and removes disorder. Providence belongs to knowledge, will, and power under different aspects, its execution being governance, and it differs from fate as the plan in God's mind from that plan realized in secondary causes.
claims: Providence adds to disposition the provision of means and removal of obstacles.
Fate is providence as realized in secondary causes.

ta-l1d39q2-Dd1e144.summary: Article 2 holds, against Democritus, Averroes, Maimonides, and the Manichaeans, that all things, singulars included, are subject to providence, each according to its nature. Incorruptible natures never fail, corruptible ones fail with their defects ordered to other natures' good, and wills can fail freely, their defects ordered to justice and others' good. Evil is foreknown and ordered, not intended. Human evil is common because of original sin and the lack of innate directing perfections, remedied by virtue as a second nature. Apparent disorders affect only external goods.
claims: Providence extends to all things according to their natures, ordering even evils to good.
Human evil is prevalent because human nature needs acquired or infused virtues.

ta-l1d39q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 39 treats divine providence. Article 1 defines providence by addition to knowledge and disposition, as provision of means to the end and removal of obstacles, distinguishing it from governance and fate. Article 2 holds that providence extends to all things, singulars included, according to their natures, ordering natural and voluntary evils to good without intending them, and explains the prevalence of human evil by original sin and human nature's need for virtue.
claims: Providence orders all things to their ends according to their natures.
Evils are foreknown and ordered to good, not intended.
